# Reproducible Pipelines with targets {#sec-targets}

Table 2 of a trial manuscript reports the primary outcome by arm,
and it was built from an analysis-set file that a cleaning script
wrote on Tuesday. On Wednesday a colleague noticed that the script
counted every patient whose outcome was never ascertained as
event-free, and fixed it. You re-ran the cleaning script and the
model, but not the script that writes Table 2, because nothing told
you to. The manuscript now reports risks from Tuesday's analysis
set beside a model fitted to Wednesday's; every number is
plausible, and no step raised an error. A dependency-aware pipeline
makes that state impossible: it knows that Table 2 depends on the
analysis set, and it rebuilds the one whenever the other changes.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Make is a tool which controls the generation of
executables and other non-source files of a program from
the program's source files.*

[Stuart Feldman]{.smallcaps}, *Make: A Program for
Maintaining Computer Programs* (1979)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::


## The dependency graph {#sec-targets-dag}

An analysis is a chain of steps: read the raw data, derive the
analysis set, summarize it, fit a model, write the report. When
you change one step, everything downstream of it becomes stale,
and everything upstream remains sound. Doing this bookkeeping by
hand means remembering which steps to re-run after every change,
and the errors it produces are silent: a table built from a stale
intermediate looks exactly like a table built from a current one.

The `targets` package [@landau2021targets] automates the
bookkeeping. You declare the steps; `targets` works out their
dependencies and order, runs only what has changed and what
depends on it, and skips the rest. It is the R successor to GNU
Make, designed around R objects rather than files. The payoff is
partly speed, but mostly trust: when `targets` reports that a
target is up to date, it reflects the current code and data,
which a hand re-run cannot promise.

The organizing idea is the [**directed acyclic graph**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-dag) (DAG). Each
step is a node; an arrow from step A to step B means B uses A's
output. 'Directed' because dependencies have a direction;
'acyclic' because a step cannot, even indirectly, depend on
itself. Given the graph, the order of execution is determined, and
so is the set of steps that a change makes stale: everything
reachable by following the arrows forward from the changed node.
@fig-targets-dag is the graph of the pipeline this chapter builds;
each node is named after its target.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-targets-dag
%%| fig-alt: "Directed acyclic graph of the HF-HOME pipeline. Two
%%|   file targets, rand_file and outcomes_file, feed the targets
%%|   randomization and outcomes. Both feed analysis_set, which
%%|   feeds table_2. A dashed arrow from table_2 to report marks the
%%|   report target added later in the chapter. Editing the
%%|   function behind analysis_set makes analysis_set, table_2, and
%%|   report stale and leaves the four targets above it untouched."
%%| fig-cap: "The dependency graph of the chapter's pipeline, with
%%|   each node named after its target. Editing the function behind
%%|   `analysis_set` makes `analysis_set`, `table_2`, and `report`
%%|   stale and leaves the four targets above it alone; `targets`
%%|   rebuilds exactly the stale nodes. The dashed `report` target
%%|   is added in @sec-targets-report."
flowchart TD
  RF["rand_file"] --> RA["randomization"]
  OF["outcomes_file"] --> OU["outcomes"]
  RA --> AS["analysis_set"]
  OU --> AS
  AS --> T2["table_2"]
  T2 -.-> REP["report"]
```

The graph is only as clear as the decomposition it encodes, and
the decomposition is yours to make, not the tool's. Make each
target a meaningful unit (read, derive, summarize, model, report),
each computed by a function with explicit inputs and one output,
rather than one thousand-line script that a single target wraps.
A target that does too much is rebuilt for every small change; a
target that does too little clutters the graph without adding
information. The finished plan is also documentation: `_targets.R`
states what depends on what, and it is often the most useful
single file for a collaborator new to the project.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In @fig-targets-dag, you edit the function behind
`table_2` and run the pipeline. Which targets are rebuilt, and
which are skipped?

**Answer.** `table_2` is rebuilt because its function changed, and
`report` because it depends on `table_2`. The two file targets,
`randomization`, `outcomes`, and `analysis_set` are skipped,
because none of them lies downstream of the change. That is the
tool's whole value: it rebuilds the two stale targets and leaves
everything upstream, which may be expensive, alone.
:::

### Exercises

1. Using @fig-targets-dag, list the targets that become stale when
   (a) a new `outcomes.csv` arrives, and (b) you edit the function
   that reads the randomization file.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) `outcomes_file`, `outcomes`, `analysis_set`, `table_2`, and
`report`: everything reachable forward from `outcomes_file`. The
randomization branch is untouched. (b) `randomization`,
`analysis_set`, `table_2`, and `report`. The function is shared by
both read targets in the pipeline below, so in that pipeline
`outcomes` is stale as well; the graph shows data dependencies,
and `targets` also tracks the functions each target calls.
:::

## A pipeline for the running study {#sec-targets-pipeline}

The pipeline reads the HF-HOME randomization list and outcomes
file, derives the analysis set, and summarizes the primary outcome
by arm as the manuscript's Table 2. The chunks below build it in a
temporary directory, so that running them changes nothing in the
book's own project; in your own work the same files live at the
root of the compendium.

```{r}
#| label: targets-project-setup
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
proj <- file.path(tempdir(), "hfhome-pipeline")
unlink(proj, recursive = TRUE)
r_dir <- file.path(proj, "R")
dir.create(r_dir, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(file.path(proj, "data"))
invisible(file.copy(
  file.path(hf_dir, c("randomization.csv", "outcomes.csv")),
  file.path(proj, "data")
))
```

### Functions in `R/`

Each step is a function in the project's `R/` directory. The
reading function keeps `patient_id` as character, because the
identifiers carry leading zeros:

```{cat}
#| label: targets-fn-read
#| engine.opts: !expr list(file = file.path(r_dir, "read.R"), lang = "r")
read_trial_csv <- function(path) {
  read_csv(path, col_types = cols(patient_id = "c", .default = "?"))
}
```

The first version of the derivation repeats Tuesday's mistake from
the opening on purpose: `coalesce()` turns a missing outcome into
'no event'.

```{cat}
#| label: targets-fn-derive-v1
#| engine.opts: !expr list(file = file.path(r_dir, "derive.R"), lang = "r")
derive_analysis_set <- function(randomization, outcomes) {
  randomization |>
    inner_join(outcomes, by = "patient_id",
               relationship = "one-to-one") |>
    mutate(
      arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health")),
      event_30d = coalesce(event_30d, 0)
    ) |>
    select(patient_id, arm, event_30d)
}
```

```{cat}
#| label: targets-fn-summarize
#| engine.opts: !expr list(file = file.path(r_dir, "summarize.R"), lang = "r")
summarize_by_arm <- function(analysis_set) {
  analysis_set |>
    summarize(
      n = n(),
      events = sum(event_30d),
      risk_pct = round(100 * mean(event_30d), 1),
      .by = arm
    ) |>
    arrange(arm)
}
```

### The plan

A `targets` project keeps its pipeline definition in a file named
`_targets.R` at the project root. The plan lists the targets; each
`tar_target()` names a step and gives the R expression that
produces it.

```{cat}
#| label: targets-plan
#| engine.opts: !expr list(file = file.path(proj, "_targets.R"), lang = "r")
library(targets)
tar_source()
tar_option_set(packages = c("readr", "dplyr"))

list(
  tar_target(rand_file, "data/randomization.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(outcomes_file, "data/outcomes.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(randomization, read_trial_csv(rand_file)),
  tar_target(outcomes, read_trial_csv(outcomes_file)),
  tar_target(analysis_set, derive_analysis_set(randomization, outcomes)),
  tar_target(table_2, summarize_by_arm(analysis_set))
)
```

`tar_source()` sources every script in `R/`. Declaring `rand_file`
and `outcomes_file` with `format = "file"` tells `targets` to watch
the files' contents, so that a new extract invalidates everything
downstream. The dependencies are not declared explicitly;
`targets` reads them from the code, noticing that `analysis_set`
uses `randomization` and `outcomes`, that `table_2` uses
`analysis_set`, and so on. That is how it builds the graph in
@fig-targets-dag without your drawing it.

`tar_option_set(packages = ...)` names the packages every
target needs. `targets` runs each target in a clean
environment, so a `library()` call at the top of a script
you sourced interactively does not carry over; packages
the functions in `R/` use must be listed here (or called
with `pkg::fn()`). The functions above call `read_csv()` and
`inner_join()` without a namespace, so without that line every
target after the file targets would fail.

### Running it

`tar_make()` runs everything that is out of date. Run it from the
project root:[^with-dir]

[^with-dir]: The chunks wrap each call in `withr::with_dir(proj,
    ...)` so that it runs in the temporary project. In a terminal
    you would start R in the project directory and type
    `tar_make()` alone.

```{r}
#| label: targets-make-first
#| eval: !expr has_targets
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_make())
```

The first run builds every target, in an order consistent with
the graph. Run it again with nothing changed:

```{r}
#| label: targets-make-second
#| eval: !expr has_targets
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_make())
```

Every target is skipped. `tar_read()` retrieves a built target
into the session, and `tar_load()` loads it under its own name:

```{r}
#| label: targets-read-v1
#| eval: !expr has_targets
table_2_v1 <- withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_read(table_2))
table_2_v1
```

Every patient randomized is in the denominator, and the risks are
diluted by the unascertained patients counted as event-free. The
table looks like any other Table 2.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Recompute the summary without `targets`, from the raw files, and
confirm that the stored target matches it. A mismatch would mean
the store holds something the current code does not produce.

```{r}
#| label: targets-verify-v1
#| eval: !expr has_targets
rand <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "randomization.csv"),
                 colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
outc <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "outcomes.csv"),
                 colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
trial <- merge(rand, outc, by = "patient_id")
events_v1 <- tapply(ifelse(is.na(trial$event_30d), 0,
                           trial$event_30d), trial$arm, sum)
stopifnot(
  nrow(trial) == nrow(rand),
  all(table_2_v1$n == table(trial$arm)[as.character(table_2_v1$arm)]),
  all(table_2_v1$events == events_v1[as.character(table_2_v1$arm)])
)
```

In your own pipeline, `tar_visnetwork()` (which needs the
`visNetwork` package) draws the graph `targets` inferred; compare
it with the one you intended.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
A model can draft the plan and the functions. What it cannot
supply is the decomposition, so give it yours.

> **Context.** An R analysis in a research compendium. Raw inputs:
> `data/randomization.csv` and `data/outcomes.csv` (one row per
> `patient_id`, a character key with leading zeros). Steps, in
> order: read each file; join them into the analysis set; summarize
> the primary outcome `event_30d` by `arm`; fit
> `glm(event_30d ~ arm, family = binomial)`.
>
> **Constraints.** One `tar_target()` per step listed, no more.
> Each target calls a function in `R/` with its inputs as
> arguments; no function reads a file path or a global variable
> directly. Declare the raw files with `format = "file"`. List the
> packages in `tar_option_set(packages = ...)`. Add no packages
> beyond `targets`, `readr`, and `dplyr`.
>
> **Criteria.** List the edges of the dependency graph you expect
> before writing code. After I run `tar_make()` twice, the second
> run skips every target.

*Failure mode.* Models collapse steps into one target that calls a
script, or have a function read `"data/outcomes.csv"` by path,
which hides the file from `targets` (the Pitfall below). *Check.*
Compare `targets::tar_network(targets_only = TRUE)$edges` with the
edge list the model gave you, and run `tar_make()` twice. The plan
and the column names are structure, not data, and may go to any
approved tool (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You delete the `tar_option_set()` line from
`_targets.R` and run `tar_make()` in a fresh session. Which
targets fail, and why does the same code work when you source the
functions and call them at the console?

**Answer.** The file targets succeed, and the first target that
calls a function from `readr` or `dplyr` fails with 'could not
find function'. Each target runs in a clean environment that sees
only the packages the plan names. At the console, `library(dplyr)`
from earlier in your session is still attached, which is exactly
the ambient state a pipeline is meant to exclude.
:::

### Exercises

2. Without running anything, list every target `table_2` depends
   on, directly or indirectly. Then confirm your list from the
   graph `targets` inferred.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Directly, `analysis_set`; indirectly, `randomization`, `outcomes`,
`rand_file`, and `outcomes_file`. `tar_network()` returns the
inferred graph without drawing it; its `edges` element lists each
arrow as a `from` and `to` pair:

```{r}
#| label: soln-10b-2
#| eval: !expr has_targets
withr::with_dir(
  proj, targets::tar_network(targets_only = TRUE)$edges
)
```
:::

## Changing a step {#sec-targets-change}

Now make Wednesday's fix: the analysis set should hold the
patients whose outcome was ascertained, with their observed
outcomes, rather than counting the missing ones as event-free.

```{cat}
#| label: targets-fn-derive-v2
#| engine.opts: !expr list(file = file.path(r_dir, "derive.R"), lang = "r")
derive_analysis_set <- function(randomization, outcomes) {
  randomization |>
    inner_join(outcomes, by = "patient_id",
               relationship = "one-to-one") |>
    filter(ascertained) |>
    mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health"))) |>
    select(patient_id, arm, event_30d)
}
```

Before running anything, ask `targets` what the edit made stale:

```{r}
#| label: targets-outdated
#| eval: !expr has_targets
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_outdated())
```

`tar_outdated()` lists the targets the next `tar_make()` will
build. Only the derivation and what lies downstream of it are
listed; the file targets and the two reads are current. Run the
pipeline:

```{r}
#| label: targets-make-after-edit
#| eval: !expr has_targets
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_make())
table_2_v2 <- withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_read(table_2))
table_2_v2
```

The two reads are skipped and the two stale targets are rebuilt.
Table 2 cannot be left behind: the fix to the derivation reached
it without your remembering it, which is the failure in the
opening made impossible. On a pipeline whose model fit takes an
hour, the same mechanism is the difference between an iteration
that costs minutes and one that costs the hour.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that the rebuilt table now counts only ascertained
patients and that the events, which the fix should not change,
are the same.

```{r}
#| label: targets-verify-v2
#| eval: !expr has_targets
obs <- trial[trial$ascertained, ]
stopifnot(
  all(table_2_v2$n == table(obs$arm)[as.character(table_2_v2$arm)]),
  all(table_2_v2$events == table_2_v1$events),
  all(table_2_v2$n < table_2_v1$n)
)
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A file read inside a function is invisible to `targets`.** If a
function opens `"data/outcomes.csv"` by its path, rather than
receiving the path from a `format = "file"` target, `targets`
tracks the function's code but not the file. Replace the file with
a new extract and `tar_outdated()` reports nothing, `tar_make()`
skips everything, and Table 2 is stale again, with the tool
vouching for it. The same holds for any global variable or
option a function reads. Pass every input as an argument, and
declare every file with `format = "file"`. Exercise 3 shows the
failure.
:::

Two further assumptions belong to you rather than to the tool.
The first is determinism: a pipeline assumes that the same inputs
produce the same outputs. `targets` gives each target its own
random-number seed, derived from the seed option
(`tar_option_set(seed = ...)`) and the target's name, so a
simulation or bootstrap target reproduces its draws however the
pipeline is scheduled; a target that reads the clock or an
unpinned package defeats that. The second is the environment: the
pipeline records code and data, not package versions, which is
the lockfile's job (@sec-renv).

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
When `targets` rebuilds more than you expected, or less, a model
can help you find the hidden dependency.

> **Context.** Below are my `_targets.R`, the functions in `R/`,
> and the output of `tar_outdated()` and of
> `tar_make()` after I changed [describe the one edit].
>
> **Constraints.** Explain using only what is in the code shown.
> Do not suggest `tar_destroy()`, `tar_invalidate()`, or deleting
> `_targets/`.
>
> **Criteria.** For each target that was rebuilt unexpectedly, or
> skipped unexpectedly, name the dependency (a function, a global
> variable, a file read by path, an option) responsible, and the
> line where it appears.

*Failure mode.* The model recommends deleting the store and
rebuilding everything, which makes the symptom disappear and
leaves the hidden dependency in place. *Check.* Make the change
the model proposes, then confirm with `tar_outdated()` that the
same edit now invalidates exactly the targets downstream of it in
@fig-targets-dag (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** After the edit, `tar_outdated()` listed
`analysis_set` and `table_2`. Suppose the edit had only renamed a
local variable inside `derive_analysis_set()`, so that the
function returns exactly the same data. Which targets would
`tar_make()` run?

**Answer.** `analysis_set` would still run, because its function's
code changed. `table_2` would then be skipped: `targets` compares
the new value of `analysis_set` with the stored one, finds them
identical, and treats everything downstream as current. A pipeline
rebuilds what a change could affect and stops where it did not.
:::

### Exercises

3. Copy the project. In the copy, delete the `outcomes_file`
   target and change the `outcomes` target to call
   `read_trial_csv("data/outcomes.csv")`, with the path written
   inside the call, and run `tar_make()`. Then remove the last row
   of `data/outcomes.csv` and ask `tar_outdated()` what is stale.
   Repeat the edit in the original project and compare.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The copy reports nothing stale after the data change; the
original reports the file target and everything downstream of it.

```{r}
#| label: soln-10b-3
#| eval: !expr has_targets
drop_last_row <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path)
  writeLines(lines[-length(lines)], path)
}

hidden <- file.path(tempdir(), "hfhome-hidden")
unlink(hidden, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(hidden)
invisible(file.copy(list.files(proj, full.names = TRUE), hidden,
                    recursive = TRUE))
unlink(file.path(hidden, "_targets"), recursive = TRUE)
plan <- readLines(file.path(hidden, "_targets.R"))
plan <- plan[!grepl("tar_target(outcomes_file", plan, fixed = TRUE)]
plan <- sub("read_trial_csv(outcomes_file)",
            "read_trial_csv(\"data/outcomes.csv\")", plan,
            fixed = TRUE)
writeLines(plan, file.path(hidden, "_targets.R"))
invisible(withr::with_dir(hidden, targets::tar_make(reporter = "silent")))

drop_last_row(file.path(hidden, "data", "outcomes.csv"))
withr::with_dir(hidden, targets::tar_outdated())

drop_last_row(file.path(proj, "data", "outcomes.csv"))
withr::with_dir(proj, targets::tar_outdated())
```

The empty result for the copy is the silent failure: the data
changed and the tool vouches that nothing did. In the original,
`outcomes_file` is a file target, so its changed contents
invalidate `outcomes`, `analysis_set`, and `table_2`.
:::

4. From `table_2` after the fix, compute the risk difference in
   percentage points, usual care minus home health, the direction
   the analysis plan uses (@sec-analysis-plan), so that a positive
   value is a reduction.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-10b-4
#| eval: !expr has_targets
risk <- setNames(table_2_v2$risk_pct, table_2_v2$arm)
risk[["Usual care"]] - risk[["Home health"]]
```

The difference is a few points in favor of home health, from
rounded risks; an estimate for the manuscript belongs in its own
target, with a confidence interval, computed from `analysis_set`
rather than from a rounded table. The analysis plan's primary
estimator is in @sec-analysis-plan.
:::

## The report as a target {#sec-targets-report}

The opening's failure ended in the manuscript, so the pipeline
should end there too. The `report` target sketched in
@fig-targets-dag would call a function of your own that renders
the document. When the report is a Quarto document, use
`tarchetypes::tar_quarto(report, "report.qmd")` instead:
it renders the document and reads the `tar_read()` and
`tar_load()` calls inside it, so the report becomes
stale whenever a target it reads changes. The addition to the plan
is two lines (display-only here, because it needs the
`tarchetypes` and `quarto` packages and a report to render):

```r
library(tarchetypes)

# appended to the list in _targets.R
tar_quarto(report, "report.qmd")
```

Inside `report.qmd`, read each result from the store rather than
recomputing it:

````qmd
```{{r}}
#| label: tbl-primary
#| tbl-cap: "Primary outcome by arm"
targets::tar_read(table_2)
```
````

A report that recomputes its numbers in its own chunks, rather
than reading them from targets, is outside the graph again:
`targets` cannot know that it depends on the analysis set, and it
can go stale exactly as Table 2 did. @sec-quarto covers the
document itself and the inline numbers it should carry.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague's `report.qmd` builds its own copy of
Table 2 in a chunk, reading the two CSV files and repeating the
derivation, instead of calling `tar_read(table_2)`. You make the
derivation fix in `R/derive.R`. What does `tar_outdated()` list,
and is the rendered report current?

**Answer.** It lists `analysis_set` and `table_2`, not `report`.
`tar_quarto()` found no `tar_read()` or `tar_load()` call in the
document, so the report depends on nothing in the pipeline, and
its copy of the derivation still holds Tuesday's mistake. The
pipeline is current and the report is not: the opening's failure,
one file later. Read every reported number from a target.
:::

### Exercises

5. Add `tar_quarto()` to a pipeline of your own with a one-table
   report, run `tar_make()`, then edit the function behind the
   table and run `tar_outdated()`. (This needs the `tarchetypes`
   and `quarto` packages and the Quarto command-line tool.)

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A correct setup lists both the table's target and `report` in
`tar_outdated()` after the edit, and `tar_make()` then re-renders
the report. If `report` is missing from the list, the document
does not read the table with `tar_read()` or `tar_load()`, so
`tar_quarto()` found no dependency on it.
:::

## Pipelines in the compendium and the container {#sec-targets-compendium}

A `targets` pipeline sits naturally inside the research
compendium of @sec-rrtools: the `_targets.R` plan and the
`R/` functions live in the package structure, `renv`
(@sec-renv) pins the packages the pipeline uses, and the
Dockerfile (@sec-docker) can end with `CMD ["Rscript",
"-e", "targets::tar_make()"]` so that running a container
from the image executes the entire analysis. `CMD` runs
when the container starts, not when the image is built;
building only prepares the environment, which is what you
want, since an image that baked in results would have to
be rebuilt for every change to the code.

The store, `_targets/`, holds every built target. Commit
`_targets.R` and the `R/` functions; keep `_targets/` out of Git,
because it is a build product that `tar_make()` regenerates. In a
container, mount the project directory so that the store outlives
the container, or every run starts from nothing.

| Piece | Holds | Version-controlled? |
|---|---|---|
| `_targets.R` | The plan: targets and their commands | Yes |
| `R/` | The functions the targets call | Yes |
| `data/raw_data/` | Inputs declared with `format = "file"` | As @sec-rrtools describes |
| `_targets/` | The store of built targets and their metadata | No |
| `renv.lock` | Package versions the pipeline runs under | Yes |

: Where a pipeline's pieces live in a compendium. {#tbl-targets-pieces}

The compendium holds the ingredients; `targets` is the recipe that
assembles them in the right order, and re-assembles only what has
changed. Together they deliver the end-to-end re-runnability that
a compendium alone only promises.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague builds the image, runs the container
without mounting the project, and reports that every run takes the
full hour. Why?

**Answer.** Without a mount, `_targets/` is written inside the
container's writable layer and discarded when the container
exits. Each run starts with an empty store, so every target is
out of date. Mount the project directory (`-v "$PWD":/work`, as in
@sec-docker) and the store persists between runs.
:::

### Exercises

6. Add a `CMD` line that runs `targets::tar_make()` to the
   canonical Dockerfile of @sec-docker-canonical, build the image,
   and run the container twice with the project mounted.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The first run's output ends with every target completed; the
second's with every target skipped. If the second run rebuilds
everything, the store is not on the mount: check that the
container's working directory is the mounted project directory,
so that `_targets/` is written to the host.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 2: derived data are a build product.** Let the pipeline
   regenerate every intermediate; never edit or hand-run one into
   place.
2. **Habit 8: a stale intermediate produces a plausible number.**
   Run `tar_outdated()` before you report anything, and pass every
   input as an argument so that it can see the change.
3. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** The pipeline tracks code and
   data; the lockfile and the container pin what it runs on.

## Cumulative practice

7. *Cumulative (uses @sec-renv).* Put this chapter's pipeline in a
   compendium of your own, with `renv` initialized. Snapshot so
   that the lockfile records `targets`, `readr`, and `dplyr`, clone
   the repository into a new directory, run `renv::restore()`, and
   confirm that `tar_make()` builds every target there and that
   `tar_read(table_2)` matches the original.
8. *On your own work (no key).* Convert a small analysis of yours
   (read, clean, model, plot) into a pipeline with one target per
   step and the functions in `R/`. Record which hidden dependencies
   on files or global variables you had to remove.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code |
|---|---|
| Source the functions in `R/` | `tar_source()` |
| Declare packages for every target | `tar_option_set(packages = c(...))` |
| Declare a target | `tar_target(name, command)` |
| Watch an input file's contents | `tar_target(f, "data/x.csv", format = "file")` |
| Run what is out of date | `tar_make()` |
| List what the next run will build | `tar_outdated()` |
| Retrieve a target | `tar_read(name)`, or `tar_load(name)` |
| Inspect the inferred graph | `tar_network()`, or `tar_visnetwork()` with `visNetwork` |
| Make a Quarto report a target | `tarchetypes::tar_quarto(report, "report.qmd")` |
| Run the pipeline in a container | `CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "targets::tar_make()"]` |

: The `targets` verbs card. {#tbl-targets-cheat-sheet}

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-10b}

1. A dependency-aware tool rebuilds exactly the steps that
   are downstream of the change and leaves the rest alone,
   and it guarantees that nothing stale survives. Re-sourcing
   all your scripts by hand either wastes time re-running
   unchanged steps or, worse, forgets a step and leaves a
   downstream result built from a stale intermediate.
2. A directed acyclic graph is a set of nodes connected by
   arrows that have a direction and form no cycles. It is
   the right abstraction because an analysis step depends on
   its inputs (direction) and cannot depend on itself
   (acyclic), so the graph determines both the execution
   order and the set of steps a change makes stale.
3. The symptom means you cannot attribute a change in
   results to a specific step, which is exactly the
   bookkeeping a pipeline tool maintains. `targets` records
   what each target depended on, so a change is always
   traceable to the step that caused it, and stale results
   never silently survive.
